title: Spatial data analysis: week 11 tutorial
text:
Week 11 — Spatial point processes
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
In this tutorial, we analyse the spatial distribution of nests of two ant species, Messor wasmanni and Cataglyphis bicolor, recorded at a site in northern Greece. The dataset ants from the spatstat.data package contains locations of 97 ant nests within a sampling window.. You can load the data using
`data(ants)` from `spatstat.data`. `plot()` shows the pattern and `summary()`
gives the window, the number of points and the average intensity.
Look at the pattern first and form an opinion before you compute anything: does
it look clustered, regular, or neither?
library(spatstat)
library(spatstat.data)
data(ants)

summary(ants)
plot(ants, main = "Spatial Point Pattern of Ant Nests", 
     cex = 0.8, pch = c(16, 17), cols = c("red", "blue"))
legend("topright", legend = c("Cataglyphis", "Messor"), 
       pch = c(16, 17), col = c("red", "blue"))
library(spatstat)
library(spatstat.data)
data(ants)

summary(ants)
plot(ants, main = "Spatial Point Pattern of Ant Nests", 
     cex = 0.8, pch = c(16, 17), cols = c("red", "blue"))
legend("topright", legend = c("Cataglyphis", "Messor"), 
       pch = c(16, 17), col = c("red", "blue"))
This summary shows that the average intensity is 0.000226 points per square unit. The proportion of Cataglyphis nests is 29.9%, Messor 70.1%. The observation window is irregularly shaped. The plot shows two types of ant nests (Cataglyphis and Messor) distributed within a polygonal study window. Messor nests are represented by blue triangles (likely pch = 17) and Cataglyphis by red dots (pch = 16).
Two complementary views. `quadratcount()` divides the window into a grid and
counts points per cell — crude but easy to test. `density.ppp()` gives a smooth
kernel estimate of the intensity surface.
The bandwidth matters: too small and you see noise, too large and you smooth the
structure away.
Q <- quadratcount(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
print(Q)
plot(ants, main="Quadrat Count of Ant Nests")
plot(Q, add=TRUE, col="red")

lambda_hat <- density(ants, bw.diggle)
plot(lambda_hat, main="Kernel Intensity Estimate of Ant Nests")
plot(ants, add=TRUE, pch=16, cex=0.5)
Q <- quadratcount(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
print(Q)
plot(ants, main="Quadrat Count of Ant Nests")
plot(Q, add=TRUE, col="red")

lambda_hat <- density(ants, bw.diggle)
plot(lambda_hat, main="Kernel Intensity Estimate of Ant Nests")
plot(ants, add=TRUE, pch=16, cex=0.5)
The quadrat counts show considerable variation in nest counts across quadrats. Some quadrats have 0 nests while others have up to 9. This suggests possible spatial inhomogeneity ### Kernel intensity estimation Let’s estimate the spatial intensity using kernel smoothing: The intensity surface shows spatial variability, with hotspots where ant nests are more concentrated. The Diggle bandwidth selector automatically chose an appropriate smoothing parameter
`ppm(ants, ~1)` fits a homogeneous Poisson process — constant intensity, points
independent. `ppm(ants, ~ x + y)` lets the log intensity vary linearly across
the window.
The second is still a Poisson process: points remain independent given the
intensity. Only the first-order structure has changed.
ppm_hom <- ppm(ants, ~1)
summary(ppm_hom)

ppm_inhom <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y)
summary(ppm_inhom)
ppm_hom <- ppm(ants, ~1)
summary(ppm_hom)

ppm_inhom <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y)
summary(ppm_inhom)
Key points are as follows: - The model assumes constant intensity across the study area - The estimated intensity is 0.000113 nests per square unit for each species - The log intensity is -9.087 with SE 0.102 - This is the simplest model, assuming no spatial trends ### Inhomogeneous Poisson process with coordinates as covariates Now we fit a model with spatial trend using x and y coordinates: Key points are as follows: - The model includes linear trends in x and y directions - Neither x nor y coefficients are statistically significant (p-values > 0.05) - The model suggests weak spatial trends at best
`quadrat.test()` compares observed and expected counts per cell. A small
p-value says the homogeneous Poisson model does not fit — but it will not tell
you whether the cause is a trend in intensity or genuine interaction between
points.
quadrat.test(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
quadrat.test(ants, nx=5, ny=5)
\(\chi^2\) = 18.512, df = 23, p-value = 0.5417 suggesting that the test does not reject CSR. However, this doesn’t account for possible inhomogeneity

title: Spatial data analysis: week 11 tutorial
text:
Challenge










`Kest()` estimates Ripley's K, and `envelope()` gives simulation bounds under
complete spatial randomness.
Above the theoretical line means clustering, below means regularity. Ant nests
compete for space, so think about which you would expect before you look.




par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Compute the K-function with Ripley correction
Kc <- Kest(ants, correction = "Ripley")

# Plot the envelope of the K-function (simulations under CSR)
plot(envelope(ants, Kest, nsim = 100), main = "K function with Envelope")

# Plot the centered K-function (difference between estimated and theoretical K)
plot(Kc$r, Kc$iso - Kc$theo, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# Compute the K-function with Ripley correction
Kc <- Kest(ants, correction = "Ripley")

# Plot the envelope of the K-function (simulations under CSR)
plot(envelope(ants, Kest, nsim = 100), main = "K function with Envelope")

# Plot the centered K-function (difference between estimated and theoretical K)
plot(Kc$r, Kc$iso - Kc$theo, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")


The observed K-function (black line) mostly falls within the CSR envelope. Some slight deviation at intermediate distances (50-100 units). There is no strong evidence of clustering or regularity. The pattern is generally consistent with CSR ### Challenge

Fit a model with a quadratic trend surface using x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2) as covariates. Compare it with the linear model.











`ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))`. The `I()` is needed so `^` means power
rather than formula-crossing.
Compare with the linear-trend fit using `AIC()`. A quadratic surface can capture
a ridge or a hollow that a plane cannot.




ppm_quad <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))
summary(ppm_quad)

AIC(ppm_inhom)
AIC(ppm_quad)
ppm_quad <- ppm(ants, ~ x + y + I(x^2) + I(y^2))
summary(ppm_quad)

AIC(ppm_inhom)
AIC(ppm_quad)


The quadratic terms are not statistically significant. AIC for linear model: 1961.509 and AIC for quadratic model: 1964.004. The simpler linear model is preferred (lower AIC)

Simulate 99 point patterns from your best model and compare their envelope with the observed K-function using envelope().











`envelope(fitted_model, Kest, nsim = 99)` simulates from the fitted model rather
than from complete spatial randomness. That is the sharper test: it asks whether
anything is left unexplained once the trend is accounted for.
If the observed K now sits inside the envelope, the inhomogeneity explained the
apparent clustering.




if (AIC(ppm_quad) < AIC(ppm_inhom)) {
  best_model <- ppm_quad
} else {
  best_model <- ppm_inhom
}
envelope_obj <- envelope(best_model, Kest, nsim=99, rank=1, verbose=FALSE)
plot(envelope_obj, main="Envelope of K-function with Simulations")
abline(a=pi, b=0, col="red", lty=2)

plot(envelope_obj$r, envelope_obj$obs - envelope_obj$mmean, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")
if (AIC(ppm_quad) < AIC(ppm_inhom)) {
  best_model <- ppm_quad
} else {
  best_model <- ppm_inhom
}
envelope_obj <- envelope(best_model, Kest, nsim=99, rank=1, verbose=FALSE)
plot(envelope_obj, main="Envelope of K-function with Simulations")
abline(a=pi, b=0, col="red", lty=2)

plot(envelope_obj$r, envelope_obj$obs - envelope_obj$mmean, type = "l", 
     xlab = "Distance r", ylab = "K(r) - CSR", main = "Deviation from CSR")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray40")


The observed K-function remains within the simulation envelope. The quadratic terms didn’t improve model fit. The spatial pattern is well-described by CSR or simple linear trend.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Week 9 — Areal data and Moran’s I
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Lip cancer data in scotland. The data contain, for each of the Scotland counties, the number of observed and expected lip cancer cases among males in Scotland between 1975-1980, and a variable that indicates the proportion of the population engaged in agriculture, fishing, or forestry (aff). The aff variable is related to exposure to sunlight which is a risk factor for lip cancer. The data also contain the shapefile of the Scotland counties and everything can be found in scotland_lip
`data(scotland_lip)` — it is already an `sf` object, so the geometry comes with
it. Look at the columns before going on.
# Read shapefile (make sure the .shp, .dbf, .shx files are all present)
scot <- scotland_lip

# View structure of the dataset
glimpse(scot)
# Read shapefile (make sure the .shp, .dbf, .shx files are all present)
scot <- scotland_lip

# View structure of the dataset
glimpse(scot)
This shapefile includes Scotland counties with observed (observed) and expected (expected) lip cancer counts and an aff variable.
The SIR is observed over expected. There is a helper: `sir(cases, expected)`.
A value above 1 means more cases than the age-sex structure of that county would
predict. Map it with a diverging scale centred on 1, so above and below are
visually distinct.
scot$SIR <- scot$cases / scot$expected

# Plot SIR using tmap
tm_shape(scot) +
  tm_fill("SIR", style = "quantile", palette = "YlOrRd", title = "SIR") +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Standardized Incidence Ratios (SIR) in Scotland")
scot$SIR <- scot$cases / scot$expected

# Plot SIR using tmap
tm_shape(scot) +
  tm_fill("SIR", style = "quantile", palette = "YlOrRd", title = "SIR") +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Standardized Incidence Ratios (SIR) in Scotland")
Red color correspond to higher SIRs, i.e., higher-than-expected lip cancer cases. Counties with SIR > 1 (darker red areas) have a higher-than-expected incidence. This could suggest localized risk factors, possibly linked to environmental or occupational exposure.
Scatter plot of SIR against `aff`. AFF is a proxy for outdoor work and hence
sunlight exposure, which is a known risk factor for lip cancer — so a positive
slope is the expected direction.
ggplot(scot, aes(x = aff, y = SIR)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "SIR vs. aff", x = "Proportion in aff", y = "SIR")
ggplot(scot, aes(x = aff, y = SIR)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "SIR vs. aff", x = "Proportion in aff", y = "SIR")
The scatter shows the plot with SIR on the y-axis and aff (proportion in agriculture, fishing, or forestry) on the x-axis. A regression line (in red) with a slight upward slope. There appears to be a weak positive association: counties with more people in aff-related jobs may have higher SIRs. This is consistent with the hypothesis that sun exposure (common in those occupations) might be linked to lip cancer risk.However, the spread is large, and correlation may not be strong without further statistical testing.
`poly2nb()` builds the neighbour list; `queen = TRUE` counts a shared corner as
adjacency, `queen = FALSE` requires a shared edge.
Scotland has islands. If a region ends up with no neighbours, that is a real
feature of the geography, not a bug — though `snap` can bridge small gaps.
nb_queen <- poly2nb(scot, queen = TRUE)
neighbor_counts <- card(nb_queen)
data.frame(county = scot$county , no_neigbours = neighbor_counts)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_queen, st_geometry(scot), main = "Queen Contiguity Neighbors", add = TRUE)
nb_queen <- poly2nb(scot, queen = TRUE)
neighbor_counts <- card(nb_queen)
data.frame(county = scot$county , no_neigbours = neighbor_counts)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_queen, st_geometry(scot), main = "Queen Contiguity Neighbors", add = TRUE)
Most counties have more than one neighbors, some with zero. The map shows the connectedness of the counties and these are essential for defining spatial weights and for modeling spatial dependence.
`card()` gives the number of neighbours per region. Find the maximum and which
county attains it.
max_n <- max(neighbor_counts)
most_connected <- scot$county[which(neighbor_counts == max_n)]
most_connected
max_n <- max(neighbor_counts)
most_connected <- scot$county[which(neighbor_counts == max_n)]
most_connected
The county with the largest number of neigbours is Perth-Kinross.
Find Wigtown's index, pull its neighbours out of the neighbour list, then map
the three categories: the county itself, its neighbours, and everywhere else.
wigtown_index <- which(scot$county == "wigtown")
wigtown_nb <- nb_queen[[wigtown_index]]
scot$neighbors <- "other"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_index] <- "area"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_nb] <- "neighbors"
ggplot(scot) + geom_sf(aes(fill = neighbors)) + theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "gray", "white"))
wigtown_index <- which(scot$county == "wigtown")
wigtown_nb <- nb_queen[[wigtown_index]]
scot$neighbors <- "other"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_index] <- "area"
scot$neighbors[wigtown_nb] <- "neighbors"
ggplot(scot) + geom_sf(aes(fill = neighbors)) + theme_bw() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "gray", "white"))
A map shows Wigtown and its neighboring counties.
`nb2mat()` with `style = "B"` for binary and `style = "W"` for row-standardised.
Row-standardised means each row sums to one, so a region with many neighbours
gives each of them less weight.
Islands with no neighbours need `zero.policy = TRUE`.
W_binary <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_binary[1:10, 1:10]

W_rowstd <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_rowstd[1:10, 1:10]
W_binary <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_binary[1:10, 1:10]

W_rowstd <- nb2mat(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
W_rowstd[1:10, 1:10]

title: Spatial data analysis: week 9 tutorial
text:
Challenge










`nb2listw()` to convert the neighbour list into weights, then `moran.test()`.
Positive Moran's I means nearby counties have similar SIRs. Check the p-value,
but also look at the statistic against its expectation, which is -1/(n-1) rather
than zero.




# Create spatial weights list
lw <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
moran.test(scot$SIR, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)
# Create spatial weights list
lw <- nb2listw(nb_queen, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
moran.test(scot$SIR, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)


Moran’s I is highly significant (p < 0.000001), indicating strong spatial autocorrelation in SIR. In plain terms: counties with high SIR tend to be near other counties with high SIR, and same for low SIR. This validates the need to account for spatial structure in modeling cancer risk. ## Challenge

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on 3 nearest neighbors and map the neighbors obtained.











`knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 3))`. Note this gives every region exactly three
neighbours, including the islands — which is either a feature or a distortion,
depending on what you think adjacency should mean.




coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(scot))
knn3 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 3)
nb_knn3 <- knn2nb(knn3)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_knn3, coords, main = "3-Nearest Neighbor Connectivity", add = T)
coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(scot))
knn3 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 3)
nb_knn3 <- knn2nb(knn3)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_knn3, coords, main = "3-Nearest Neighbor Connectivity", add = T)


Each county is connected to its 3 closest neighbors by distance. Useful when physical proximity is more important than shared boundaries (e.g., for air pollution, etc.).

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on distance and map the neighbors obtained.











`dnearneigh()` takes a lower and upper distance bound. The geometry is in
metres, so the bounds must be too.




dists <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 50)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(dists, coords, main = "Distance-Based Neighbors", add= T)
dists <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = 50)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(dists, coords, main = "Distance-Based Neighbors", add= T)


Counties within the distance of 50 to each other are connected. Allows flexible neighborhood structures based on absolute proximity. May capture spatial spillover more naturally than contiguity in some contexts.

Calculate the neighbors of each of the regions of Scotland based on contiguity Neighbors of order 2 and map the neighbors obtained.











`nblag()` gives higher-order neighbours. Order 2 means "neighbours of my
neighbours", which widens the definition of local considerably.




nb_order2 <- nblag(nb_queen, 2)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_order2[[2]], coords, main = "Second-Order Queen Neighbors", add = T)
nb_order2 <- nblag(nb_queen, 2)
plot(st_geometry(scot), border = "lightgray")
plot(nb_order2[[2]], coords, main = "Second-Order Queen Neighbors", add = T)


This visualizes neighbors-of-neighbors.

Construct the spatial weights matrix using inverse distance values.











Compute inverse distances between centroids, then pass them to `nb2mat()` via
`glist`. Closer neighbours then carry more weight than distant ones.




distances <- nbdists(nb_queen, coords)
inv_dists <- lapply(distances, function(x) 1/x)
lw_inv <- nb2mat(nb_queen, glist = inv_dists, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw_inv[1:10, 1:10]
distances <- nbdists(nb_queen, coords)
inv_dists <- lapply(distances, function(x) 1/x)
lw_inv <- nb2mat(nb_queen, glist = inv_dists, style = "B", zero.policy = TRUE)
lw_inv[1:10, 1:10]


We are showing a few rows and columns of the spatial weight matrix based on inverse distance. Closer neighbors have more influence, farther ones less.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 7 tutorial
text:
Week 7 — Geostatistics and variograms
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Galicia dataset, often used in geostatistical analysis, refers to lead concentration data from a network of meteorological stations across the Galicia region in Northwest Spain. The Galicia dataset has the following columns:
`data(galicia)`. Five columns: the lead concentration and its log, the
coordinates, and PM10. Check which is which before you go further — you will be
modelling the log, not the raw concentration.
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# View the first few rows
head(galicia)
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# View the first few rows
head(galicia)
The dataset contains 5 variables: - lead: measured lead concentration - loglead: log-transformed lead - long, lat: geographic coordinates - pm10: pollutant levels This is the basic EDA (exploratory data analysis) step. Always check variable types and completeness first.
Turn the data frame into an `sf` object with `st_as_sf()`, telling it which
columns hold the coordinates and what CRS they are in (these are longitude and
latitude, so EPSG:4326).
Then map it. When you look at the map, ask where the stations are — is the
design regular, clustered, or opportunistic? That governs what you can estimate.
# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

# Map the lead concentration
tm_shape(galicia_sf) +
  tm_symbols(col = "lead", palette = "viridis", style = "quantile",
             title.col = "Lead conc.") +
  tm_layout(title = "")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = galicia_sf, aes(color = lead), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Lead Concentration in Galicia", color = "Lead") +
  theme_minimal()
# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

# Map the lead concentration
tm_shape(galicia_sf) +
  tm_symbols(col = "lead", palette = "viridis", style = "quantile",
             title.col = "Lead conc.") +
  tm_layout(title = "")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = galicia_sf, aes(color = lead), size = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  labs(title = "Lead Concentration in Galicia", color = "Lead") +
  theme_minimal()
Converts the data to a spatial object and plots spatial locations with colors indicating lead concentration. I have provided two ways of mapping the data, you can always use the one that you found interesting and easy.
An ordinary scatter plot of `loglead` against `pm10`, with a fitted line.
Both are products of traffic and industry, so a positive association would not
be surprising.
ggplot(galicia, aes(x = pm10, y = loglead)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of log(lead) vs PM10", x = "PM10", y = "Log(Lead)") +
  theme_minimal()
ggplot(galicia, aes(x = pm10, y = loglead)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of log(lead) vs PM10", x = "PM10", y = "Log(Lead)") +
  theme_minimal()
If there’s a visible trend and a linear fit, then PM10 is a meaningful predictor. In your case, a clear positive trend suggests so.
Fit `lm(loglead ~ pm10)` first, then build the variogram of its **residuals** —
not of the raw response. The variogram of the response would confound spatial
structure with the trend the covariate explains.
Add a Monte Carlo envelope so you can judge whether the shape is more than noise.
lm1 <- lm(loglead ~ pm10, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid <- residuals(lm1)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)

galicia_variog <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
lm1 <- lm(loglead ~ pm10, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid <- residuals(lm1)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)

galicia_variog <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
A variogram shows how data points are correlated over distance. After removing the effect of PM10 (via regression), we assess the spatial structure in residuals. The variogram rises with distance, meaning that there’s spatial correlation. The envelope via permutation helps confirm if observed structure is statistically significant. In this case, the observed spatial correlation is significant as the some of the empirical semi-variogram (dots) lies outside the Monte Carlo envelopes.
Repeat with `lm(loglead ~ 1)`, that is with no covariate.
Compare the two variograms. If removing the covariate makes the variogram rise
more steeply, the covariate was explaining part of what otherwise looks like
spatial correlation.
lm2 <- lm(loglead ~ 1, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid2 <- residuals(lm2)

galicia_variog2 <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid2",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
lm2 <- lm(loglead ~ 1, data = galicia)
galicia_sf$resid2 <- residuals(lm2)

galicia_variog2 <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid2",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 1000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2)


plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog2,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
We repeat the variogram, this time without adjusting for PM10. The spatial structure appears stronger here than before, it confirms that PM10 explains some spatial pattern.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 7 tutorial
text:
Challenge
Using the dataset named loaloa, Fit an appropriate model and examine the residual for the evidence of spatial correlation. This dataset is from Loaloa prevalence survey collected in Cameroon and some part of Nigeria. Hint: Repeat the task in question 1 to 6. To learn more about the data, read the readme file named “ReadMe_loaloa.txt”










The envelope test permutes the residuals across locations many times. Under the
null of no spatial correlation, location is irrelevant, so a permuted variogram
is as good as the real one.
The observed curve lying outside the envelope at short distances is evidence of
spatial correlation. Try changing the number of permutations and see how stable
your conclusion is.




### Increase the number of permulation
galicia_variog3 <- s_variogram(data = galicia_sf,
                              variable = "resid2",
                              scale_to_km = TRUE,
                              n_permutation = 10000)

plot_s_variogram(galicia_variog3,
                 plot_envelope = TRUE)
### Increase the number of permulation

                 plot_envelope = TRUE)

This dataset is from Loaloa prevalence survey collected in Cameroon and some part of Nigeria. Hint: Repeat the task in question 1 to 6.

We first assessed the effect of the available predictors and then identified the most relevant subset of predictors for the model using stepwise regression. NoteHow to use this page

Q1: For the fev1 data, consider a linear mixed model of the form [ ( ){ij} = 0 + 1 {ij} + b{0i} + b{1i} {ij} + {ij}, ] where \(\log\left( \frac{\text{FEV}_1}{\text{Height}} \right)_{ij}\): the response for individual \(i\) at time \(j\) \(\beta_0\): fixed intercept \(\beta_1\): fixed slope for age \(b_{0i}\): random intercept for individual \(i\), capturing between-subject variation \(b_{1i}\): random slope for age for individual \(i\) \(\varepsilon_{ij}\): within-subject residual error. Note that \(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) and \(\varepsilon_{i}) \sim N(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\).

Express the above model in matrix form and explain the corresponding matrices/vectors.

Write the \(n_i\) observations on girl \(i\) as a vector and stack the fixed and random parts:
\[\mathbf{Y}_i = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{b}_i + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i,
\qquad i = 1,\dots,m,\]
where, for girl \(i\) measured at ages \(a_{i1},\dots,a_{in_i}\):

\(\mathbf{Y}_i\) is the \(n_i \times 1\) response vector, with \(j\)th element \(\log(\text{FEV}_1/\text{Height})_{ij}\).
\(\mathbf{X}_i\) is the \(n_i \times 2\) fixed-effects design matrix \[\mathbf{X}_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & a_{i1} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & a_{in_i}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0, \beta_1)^{\mathrm{T}}.\] \(\beta_0\) is the population mean response at age zero and \(\beta_1\) the population mean change per year of age. These are the same for every girl.
\(\mathbf{Z}_i\) is the \(n_i \times 2\) random-effects design matrix. Here the model has a random intercept and a random slope in age, so \(\mathbf{Z}_i = \mathbf{X}_i\), and \(\mathbf{b}_i = (b_{0i}, b_{1i})^{\mathrm{T}}\) is girl \(i\)’s departure from the population intercept and slope.
\(\mathbf{b}_i \sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) with \[\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_0^2 & \sigma_{01} \\ \sigma_{01} & \sigma_1^2 \end{pmatrix},\] the between-subject covariance matrix. \(\sigma_0^2\) is the variance of individual intercepts, \(\sigma_1^2\) the variance of individual slopes, and \(\sigma_{01}\) their covariance — positive if girls who start higher also grow faster.
\(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \sim N_{n_i}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_i)\) is the within-subject error, independent of \(\mathbf{b}_i\). \(\mathbf{R}_i\) is \(n_i \times n_i\) and its structure is what parts 2.1–2.4 ask you to choose: \(\sigma^2\mathbf{I}\) for independence, compound symmetry, AR(1), or ARMA(1,1).

Marginally, integrating out the random effects,
\[\mathbf{Y}_i \sim N_{n_i}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta},\;
\mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf{R}_i\right).\]
This is the key point of the whole model: correlation between two measurements on the same girl arises from two sources — the shared random effects \(\mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\), and any serial correlation in \(\mathbf{R}_i\). Measurements on different girls are independent, because they share neither.
Note that \(n_i\) varies between girls: the data are unbalanced, so the matrices differ in dimension from one girl to the next. This is why the model is written per subject rather than as one \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \dots\) for the whole sample.

In R, use the function `lme( )’ to analyze the data by specifying \(\mathbf{G}\) as general covariance structure and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) as












`groupedData()` first: it tells `nlme` which column identifies the subject, so
`logfev1_ht ~ age | id`.
Then one `lme()` per structure. The mean model and `random =` stay the same
throughout — only `correlation =` changes. The four you need are: nothing at all
(independence), `corCompSymm`, `corAR1` and `corARMA(p = 1, q = 1)`.
Use `method = "ML"`, because you are about to compare models that differ in
their fixed or covariance structure.




library(nlme)
library(tidyverse)
data <- fev1
data.grouped <- groupedData(logfev1_ht~age| id, data=data, FUN=mean)
# Independent (Ri): no correlation between residuals
fit_ind <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
               random = ~ 1 | id,
               correlation = NULL, 
               data = data.grouped, 
               method = "ML")

# Compound Symmetry (Ri): equal correlation (exchangeable)
fit_cs <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
              random = ~ 1 | id,
              correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), 
              data = data.grouped, 
              method = "ML")

# AR(1): autocorrelated residuals
fit_ar1 <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
               random = ~ 1 | id,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id), 
               data = data.grouped, 
               method = "ML")

# ARMA(1,1)
fit_arma11 <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                  random = ~ 1 | id,
                  correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 1, form = ~ 1 | id), 
                  data = data.grouped, 
                  method = "ML")

library(tidyverse)
data <- fev1
data.grouped <- groupedData(logfev1_ht~age| id, data=data, FUN=mean)
# Independent (Ri): no correlation between residuals
fit_ind <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
               random = ~ 1 | id,
               correlation = NULL, 
               data = data.grouped, 
               method = "ML")

# Compound Symmetry (Ri): equal correlation (exchangeable)
fit_cs <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
              random = ~ 1 | id,
              correlation = corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | id), 
              data = data.grouped, 
              method = "ML")

# AR(1): autocorrelated residuals
fit_ar1 <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
               random = ~ 1 | id,
               correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id), 
               data = data.grouped, 
               method = "ML")

# ARMA(1,1)
fit_arma11 <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                  random = ~ 1 | id,
                  correlation = corARMA(p = 1, q = 1, form = ~ 1 | id), 
                  data = data.grouped, 
                  method = "ML")


2.1. independent covariance structure,\
2.2. compound symmetry covariance structure,\
2.3. AR(1) structure,\
2.4. ARMA(1,1) structure,
where the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.










`AIC()` and `BIC()` both accept several fitted models at once and return a table.
Lower is better for both. If they disagree, remember BIC penalises extra
parameters harder.




AIC(fit_ind, fit_cs, fit_ar1, fit_arma11)
BIC(fit_ind, fit_cs, fit_ar1, fit_arma11)
AIC(fit_ind, fit_cs, fit_ar1, fit_arma11)
BIC(fit_ind, fit_cs, fit_ar1, fit_arma11)


The AR(1) model has the lowest AIC and BIC, meaning it best captures the within-individual correlation over time. AR(1) assumes that measurements closer in time are more strongly correlated, which is sensible for lung function data collected annually.

With the selected structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\), select the best structure for \(\mathbf{G}\) among the candidates below:












Same idea as item 3, but now `correlation =` is held at whatever you selected
and `random =` is what varies.
The three candidates are `pdIdent(~ age)`, `pdDiag(~ age)` and a general
covariance, which is `nlme`'s default when you write `random = ~ age | id`.




# G as independent (identity)
fit_G_ind <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                 random = pdIdent(~ age),
                 correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                 data = data.grouped, 
                 method = "ML")

# G as diagonal
fit_G_diag <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                  random = pdDiag(~ age),
                  correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                  data = data.grouped, 
                  method = "ML")

# G as general
fit_G_gen <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                 random = pdSymm(~ age),
                 correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                 data = data.grouped, 
                 method = "ML")
# G as independent (identity)
fit_G_ind <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                 random = pdIdent(~ age),
                 correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                 data = data.grouped, 
                 method = "ML")

# G as diagonal
fit_G_diag <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                  random = pdDiag(~ age),
                  correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                  data = data.grouped, 
                  method = "ML")

# G as general
fit_G_gen <- lme(logfev1_ht ~ age, 
                 random = pdSymm(~ age),
                 correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1 | id),
                 data = data.grouped, 
                 method = "ML")


3.1. independent covariance structure,\
3.2. diagonal covariance structure,\
3.3. general covariance structure.
Again, the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.










Compare the three G structures the same way you compared the R structures.




AIC(fit_G_ind, fit_G_diag, fit_G_gen)
BIC(fit_G_ind, fit_G_diag, fit_G_gen)
AIC(fit_G_ind, fit_G_diag, fit_G_gen)
BIC(fit_G_ind, fit_G_diag, fit_G_gen)


The diagonal structure (fit_G_diag) has the lowest AIC and BIC. A diagonal random effects structure means that the intercept and slope vary independently between individuals (i.e., no covariance between random intercept and random slope). The best model uses AR(1) for residuals and diagonal structure for random effects G.

For your overall best model, interpret the parameters of the model.










































–>






















`summary()` on the winning fit. Read three things: the fixed effects (what is
the average growth rate?), the random effects table (how much do girls differ in
intercept and slope?), and the residual standard deviation.
Try to state each in a sentence about lung function, not about the model.




summary(fit_G_diag)
summary(fit_G_diag)


Interpretion of the parameters of the model #### Fixed effect The model estimates the average log(FEV1/height) at age 0 to be -0.32 (though age 0 is outside the range of observed data- it’s just a baseline). For every 1-year increase in age, the log(FEV1/height) increases by approximately 0.058. This indicates growth in lung function relative to height over time, which is expected during adolescence. #### Random effect Individuals differ in both their baseline lung function (intercept) and rate of growth (slope). The variation in intercept is much larger than the variation in slope (0.0853 vs 0.0019), suggesting that most differences between individuals are in their starting level, not growth rate.
#### Random error There is a moderate autocorrelation in the residuals—observations closer in time are positively correlated, which supports the use of AR(1). This value of 0.62 implies a reasonable memory over time within individuals.

pairs(cattle[, -1], main='All Cattle Data')


There is linear correlation overall, which reduces for increasing lag. The lag-\(1\) linear correlation is very strong, so cattle weight measurements between successive time points exhibit strong linear correlation.

Divide the cattle dataset into two groups, Group A and Group B. For each group, determine the sample means at each time point, as well as the sample covariance and sample correlation.











`which(cattle[, 1] == 0)` gives the row numbers for one group. Use that to

Produce pairwise scatter plots for each group. Identify and discuss any similarities or differences between the two groups evident in the plots.











You already have the two group subsets from item 6, so this is `pairs()` twice.
Give each a `main` title so you can tell them apart.




pairs(a.cattle, main='Group A Cattle Data')

pairs(b.cattle, main='Group B Cattle Data')


The scatter plots show similar correlation structure between the two groups. Group A exhibits slightly stronger linear correlation than group B overall.

Plot the sample means of both groups against time within a single figure. Provide your interpretations and conclusions drawn from the figure.











Plot the first group's means with `plot()`, then add the second with `lines()`
in a different colour. Both means are vectors of length 11 that you computed in
item 6.




# Plot the sample means of both groups over time
plot(
  time, am.timepoint, type='l', ylab='Mean Weight (KG)', lwd=2,
  main='Mean Weight (KG) - Group A (Black) and Group B (Red)'

lines(time, bm.timepoint, col=2, lwd=2) # Use color red for Group B

The sample means for the two groups are similar, thus having strong linear correlation. The mean weight of group A is initially higher than the mean weight of group B. However, the mean weight of group A starts to decrease after time 4, while the mean weight of group B remains relatively constant. By time 10, the mean weight of group B is higher than the mean weight of group A.
Q2 You will work with longitudinal data on lung function growth in school-age girls from Topeka, Kansas, as part of the Six Cities Study of Air Pollution and Health. The dataset contains repeated pulmonary function measurements from 299 girls, typically enrolled around ages 6-10 and followed annually until high school graduation or loss to follow-up. The number of observations per individual ranges from 1 to 12, making the dataset unbalanced with respect to age.
At each visit, lung function was measured using simple spirometry, and the outcome of interest is the logarithm of the ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) to height, i.e., log(FEV1/height).
The dataset is available in the course package.
Key variables include:
- id: unique identifier for each girl
- ht: height (m)
- age: age at measurement (years)
- baseht: height at the first visit
- baseage: age at the first visit
- fev1: volume of air exhaled in the first second (litres)
- logfev1: logarithm of fev1
- logfev1_ht: pre-computed log(fev1/height)
  

Load the dataset and check the structure of the data. How many observations are there in total? How many individuals?











`fev1` is in long format: one row per visit, not per girl. So `nrow()` is the
number of observations, and the number of girls is the number of distinct `id`
values.




require(tidyverse)
require(ggplot2)
data <- fev1
# View structure and a quick summary
str(data)
summary(data)

# Number of observations (rows)
n_obs <- nrow(data)

# Number of unique individuals

cat("Total observations:", n_obs, "\n")

require(tidyverse)

This step confirms that we’re working with a longitudinal dataset, each girl contributes multiple measurements over time. However, the number of measurements varies per individual, which means the data is unbalanced.

Summarise the number of observations per individual. What does this tell you about the balance of the data?











Count the rows per `id`, then summarise those counts. A histogram of them shows
the shape of the follow-up.
If every girl had the same count, the data would be balanced — what do you see?




# Count observations per individual
obs_per_individual <- data %>%
  count(id)

# Summary statistics
summary(obs_per_individual$n)

# Plot a histogram
ggplot(obs_per_individual, aes(x = n)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "skyblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Number of Observations per Individual",
    x = "Number of Observations",
    y = "Count of Individuals"
  )
# Count observations per individual
obs_per_individual <- data %>%
  count(id)

# Summary statistics
summary(obs_per_individual$n)

# Plot a histogram
ggplot(obs_per_individual, aes(x = n)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "skyblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Number of Observations per Individual",
    x = "Number of Observations",
    y = "Count of Individuals"
  )


The histogram shows a right-skewed distribution, meaning most girls have moderate to high follow-up, but a few have very few observations (e.g., just 1–2).

Produce a plot of log(fev1 / height) against age for 50 randomly selected girls. Connect points for the same individual. Comment on the variability between individuals and the measurement patterns over age.











Draw a random sample of `id` values first, then keep only the rows belonging to
them. In `ggplot`, `group = id` is what stops the lines being joined into one
long zigzag across girls.
Set a seed so your plot is reproducible.




# Sample 50 random individuals
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility
sample_ids <- sample(unique(data$id), 50)

data_sample <- data %>%
  filter(id %in% sample_ids)

# Plot
ggplot(data_sample, aes(x = age, y = logfev1_ht, group = id, color = factor(id))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "log(FEV1 / height) vs Age for 50 Randomly Selected Girls",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "log(FEV1 / height)",
    color = "Individual ID"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
# Sample 50 random individuals
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility
sample_ids <- sample(unique(data$id), 50)

data_sample <- data %>%
  filter(id %in% sample_ids)

# Plot
ggplot(data_sample, aes(x = age, y = logfev1_ht, group = id, color = factor(id))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "log(FEV1 / height) vs Age for 50 Randomly Selected Girls",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "log(FEV1 / height)",
    color = "Individual ID"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


This plot is a classic spaghetti plot used in longitudinal analysis. There is substantial between-person variability, some girls show steep increases, others plateau. Measurement times are irregular, highlighting the unbalanced design. Some trajectories are short, these are girls with only a few data points.

Compute and plot the average log(fev1 / height) at each age, aggregating across individuals.











Group by `age` and take the mean of `logfev1_ht` within each. Plotting the
result gives the population-average growth curve.
Ages are not on a common grid, so some ages are supported by very few girls —
worth bearing in mind when you read the plot.




# Group by age and compute mean logfev1/ht
mean_by_age <- data %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(mean_logfev1_ht = mean(logfev1_ht, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())

# Plot
ggplot(mean_by_age, aes(x = age, y = mean_logfev1_ht)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred") +
  # geom_line(color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Average log(FEV1 / height) vs Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Mean log(FEV1 / height)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
# Group by age and compute mean logfev1/ht
mean_by_age <- data %>%
  group_by(age) %>%
  summarise(mean_logfev1_ht = mean(logfev1_ht, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n())

# Plot
ggplot(mean_by_age, aes(x = age, y = mean_logfev1_ht)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkred") +
  # geom_line(color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "Average log(FEV1 / height) vs Age",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Mean log(FEV1 / height)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


This gives us a population-level view of lung function growth over age. The plot shows a gradual increase in lung function (adjusted for height), which is expected during adolescence. However, since age is a continuous variable and girls were not all measured at the same ages, the data is sparse at some ages, causing potential noise in the mean trend. A smoothed line (e.g., LOESS or spline) could help to further clarify the trend.

title: Longitudinal Data Analysis: week 3 tutorial
text:
Week 3 — Estimation and inference






NoteHow to use this page





Each exercise below is a live R session. Type your answer and press Run; you can experiment freely, nothing is saved and nothing can break. The first block takes a few seconds to start while R loads in your browser.
Worked solutions are on Canvas.



























Q1: For the cattle data, use the linear mixed model with random intercept and random slope in Day: to model the bodyweight growth of cattle over the observation period, where \(\mathbf{b}_i\)=\((b_{i1},b_{i2})'\sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G})\) with \(\mathbf{G}\) being (\(2\times 2\)) positive definite and \(\varepsilon_i=(\varepsilon_{i1},...,\varepsilon_{i11})'\sim
N_{11}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{R}_i)\) with \(\mathbf{R}_i\) being (\(11\times
11\)) positive definite.










`groupedData()` needs the response, the time variable and the subject
identifier: `Y ~ day | subject`. The cattle data are wide, so you will need to
reshape to long form first.




# Load nlme package

library(nlme)

# Load cattle data
# 60 subjects, 30 per group
# 11 measurements per subject

cattle_data <- cattle

# Define response as a vector (matrix of one column)

Y <- matrix(t(cattle_data[, 2:12]), ncol=1)

# Define a vector (matrix of one column) that indicates the subject of each measurement

subject <- matrix(rep(1:60, each=11), ncol=1)

# Define a vector that indicates the type of treatment (group) for each subject

treatment <- factor(rep(c('A', 'B'), each=330))

# Reorder levels of treatment

treatment <- relevel(treatment, ref="B")

# Define days at which measurements are collected

day <- rep(c(0, 14, 28, 42, 56, 70, 84, 98, 112, 126, 133), 60)

# Place constructed variables in a data frame

cattle  <- data.frame(subject, Y, day, treatment)

# Construct groupedData object, attaching the formula as an attribute to the data

cattle.grouped <- groupedData(Y~day | subject, data=cattle, FUN=mean, outer=~treatment)
# Load nlme package

library(nlme)

# Load cattle data
# 60 subjects, 30 per group
# 11 measurements per subject

cattle_data <- cattle

# Define response as a vector (matrix of one column)

Y <- matrix(t(cattle_data[, 2:12]), ncol=1)

# Define a vector (matrix of one column) that indicates the subject of each measurement

subject <- matrix(rep(1:60, each=11), ncol=1)

# Define a vector that indicates the type of treatment (group) for each subject

treatment <- factor(rep(c('A', 'B'), each=330))

# Reorder levels of treatment

treatment <- relevel(treatment, ref="B")

# Define days at which measurements are collected

day <- rep(c(0, 14, 28, 42, 56, 70, 84, 98, 112, 126, 133), 60)

# Place constructed variables in a data frame

cattle  <- data.frame(subject, Y, day, treatment)

# Construct groupedData object, attaching the formula as an attribute to the data

cattle.grouped <- groupedData(Y~day | subject, data=cattle, FUN=mean, outer=~treatment)



Express the above model in matrix form and explain the corresponding matrices/vectors.

The scalar model is
\[Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Day}_j + \beta_2 \text{Treatment}_i
+ \beta_3\,\text{Day}_j\!\times\!\text{Treatment}_i + b_{i1} + \text{Day}_j\, b_{i2}
+ \varepsilon_{ij}.\]
Collecting the \(11\) observations on animal \(i\) gives
\[\mathbf{Y}_i = \mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta} + \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{b}_i
+ \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,60,\]
with the following pieces.
Response. \(\mathbf{Y}_i = (Y_{i1},\dots,Y_{i,11})^{\mathrm{T}}\), the \(11 \times 1\) vector of bodyweights for animal \(i\).
Fixed effects. \(\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)^{\mathrm{T}}\) and \(\mathbf{X}_i\) is \(11 \times 4\). Writing \(t_j\) for the \(j\)th measurement day and \(T_i \in \{0,1\}\) for the treatment indicator of animal \(i\),
\[\mathbf{X}_i = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & t_1 & T_i & t_1 T_i \\
1 & t_2 & T_i & t_2 T_i \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & t_{11} & T_i & t_{11} T_i
\end{pmatrix}.\]
Because \(T_i\) does not change within an animal, its column is constant down \(\mathbf{X}_i\). The interpretation is: \(\beta_0\) the intercept for the reference group, \(\beta_1\) its growth rate per day, \(\beta_2\) the difference in intercept between groups, and \(\beta_3\) the difference in growth rate — the parameter the experiment exists to estimate.
Random effects. \(\mathbf{b}_i = (b_{i1}, b_{i2})^{\mathrm{T}}\) is \(2 \times 1\) and
\[\mathbf{Z}_i = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & t_1 \\ 1 & t_2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & t_{11} \end{pmatrix}
\quad (11 \times 2),\]
so each animal has its own intercept and its own slope in day, drawn from
\[\mathbf{b}_i \sim N_2(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{G}), \qquad
\mathbf{G} = \begin{pmatrix} g_{11} & g_{12} \\ g_{12} & g_{22} \end{pmatrix}
\ \text{positive definite}.\]
\(\mathbf{G}\) is the between-animal covariance: \(g_{11}\) how much animals differ in starting weight, \(g_{22}\) how much they differ in growth rate, \(g_{12}\) whether the two are related.
Errors. \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_i \sim N_{11}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_i)\), independent of \(\mathbf{b}_i\), with \(\mathbf{R}_i\) an \(11\times 11\) positive definite matrix describing within-animal variation not explained by the random effects — measurement error plus any serial correlation.
Marginal distribution. Integrating out \(\mathbf{b}_i\),
\[\mathbf{Y}_i \sim N_{11}\!\left(\mathbf{X}_i\boldsymbol{\beta},\;
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\right), \qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf{R}_i.\]
Two remarks worth making explicitly:

Even if \(\mathbf{R}_i = \sigma^2\mathbf{I}\), the responses on one animal are still correlated, because \(\mathbf{Z}_i\mathbf{G}\mathbf{Z}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\) is not diagonal. The random effects alone induce within-animal correlation.
With a random slope, that induced correlation is not stationary: the variance \(\mathbf{z}_j^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{z}_j + R_{i,jj}\) grows with \(t_j\), since \(\mathbf{z}_j = (1, t_j)^{\mathrm{T}}\). Animals fan out over time. This is why the random-slope model often fits growth data better than a random intercept alone.

The design here is balanced — all 60 animals are measured on the same 11 days — so \(\mathbf{X}_i\), \(\mathbf{Z}_i\) and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) have the same dimensions for every \(i\), and \(\mathbf{Z}_i\) is in fact the same matrix for all animals.

In R, use the function `lme( )’ to analyze the data by specifying \(\mathbf{G}\) as general covariance structure and \(\mathbf{R}_i\) as
2.1. independent covariance structure,












The independent structure is the default: give `lme()` no `correlation`
argument at all. Keep `random = ~ day | subject` so G stays general.




lme.un.ide <- lme(Y ~ day * treatment, data=cattle.grouped, random=~day | subject, method="ML")

summary(lme.un.ide)
lme.un.ide <- lme(Y ~ day * treatment, data=cattle.grouped, random=~day | subject, method="ML")

summary(lme.un.ide)


2.2. compound symmetry covariance structure,\










`update()` saves retyping the whole call — pass only what changes.
Compound symmetry is `corCompSymm(form = ~ 1 | subject)`: every pair of times
equally correlated, however far apart.




lme.un.cs <- update(lme.un.ide, correlation=corCompSymm(form=~1|subject))

summary(lme.un.cs)
lme.un.cs <- update(lme.un.ide, correlation=corCompSymm(form=~1|subject))

summary(lme.un.cs)


2.3. AR(1) structure,\










`corAR1(form = ~ day | subject)`. Correlation now decays geometrically with the
gap in days, which is usually more plausible for growth data than compound
symmetry.




lme.un.AR1 <- update(lme.un.ide, correlation=corAR1(form=~day | subject))

summary(lme.un.AR1)
lme.un.AR1 <- update(lme.un.ide, correlation=corAR1(form=~day | subject))

summary(lme.un.AR1)


2.4. ARMA(1,1) structure,
where the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method. Select the best structure of \(\mathbf{R}_i\) in terms of the resulting AIC or BIC value.










`corARMA` needs both orders: `p = 1, q = 1`.
Then `anova()` on all four fits gives the comparison. They are nested, so the
likelihood ratio tests in that table are meaningful.




lme.un.ARMA <- update(lme.un.ide,correlation=corARMA(form=~day | subject, p=1, q=1))

summary(lme.un.ARMA)

anova(lme.un.ide, lme.un.cs, lme.un.AR1, lme.un.ARMA)
lme.un.ARMA <- update(lme.un.ide,correlation=corARMA(form=~day | subject, p=1, q=1))

summary(lme.un.ARMA)

anova(lme.un.ide, lme.un.cs, lme.un.AR1, lme.un.ARMA)


Now, we compare models with different covariance structures \(\mathbf{R}_i\) The observation times (variable ) are not equally spaced. To use an AR(1) structure with unequally spaced times, the correlation option being set as . On the other hand, , treats the observation times as equally spaced, and this is why it is not used. Similarly, for the ARMA(1,1) structure, we use the option

With the selected structure for \(\mathbf{R}_i\), select the best structure for \(\mathbf{G}\) among the candidates below:
3.1. independent covariance structure,












Now hold `correlation` fixed and vary `random`. `pdIdent(~ day)` forces the
random intercept and slope to have equal variance and zero covariance — the most
restrictive of the three.




lme.ide.ide <- update(lme.un.ide, random=pdIdent(~day))

summary(lme.ide.ide)
lme.ide.ide <- update(lme.un.ide, random=pdIdent(~day))

summary(lme.ide.ide)


3.2. diagonal covariance structure,\










`pdDiag(~ day)` allows different variances but still no covariance between the
random intercept and slope.




lme.diag.ide <- update(lme.un.ide, random=pdDiag(~day))

summary(lme.diag.ide)
lme.diag.ide <- update(lme.un.ide, random=pdDiag(~day))

summary(lme.diag.ide)


3.3. general covariance structure.
Again, the option `method’ in R is the maximum likelihood (ML) estimation method.










The general structure is the unrestricted one you already fitted. Compare all
three with `anova()`.




summary(lme.un.ide)

anova(lme.un.ide, lme.ide.ide, lme.diag.ide)
summary(lme.un.ide)

anova(lme.un.ide, lme.ide.ide, lme.diag.ide)


Now, we compare models with different covariance structures \(\mathbf{R}_i\) When \(G\) takes a diagonal covariance structure, the model has smallest AIC/BIC value. We then select the diagonal covariance structure as the best structure for \(G\).

Refit the selected model so far, but using the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation method this time.











Refit with `method = "REML"`. ML underestimates variance components because it
ignores the degrees of freedom used estimating the fixed effects; REML corrects
for that. Now that the structure is settled, REML gives better variance
estimates.
Try `run_app("lmm_simulator")` with a small number of subjects to watch this
happen.




lme.diag.ide.REML <- update(lme.diag.ide, method="REML")

summary(lme.diag.ide.REML)
lme.diag.ide.REML <- update(lme.diag.ide, method="REML")

summary(lme.diag.ide.REML)



Based on the selected model, fitted using the REML method, answer the following questions:
5.1. Produce the standardized residuals plot (i.e., residuals against fitted values) and the residual qqnorm plot. Justify whether the fitted model is good.












Two plots. The first is standardised residuals against fitted values — look for
constant spread. The second is a normal QQ plot of those residuals.
`plot(fit, resid(., type = "p") ~ fitted(.))` gives the first.




plot(lme.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.), id=0.05, adj=-0.1)

qqnorm(lme.diag.ide.REML, ~ resid(.))

lme2.diag.ide.REML <- update(lme.diag.ide,method="REML", ~.+I(day^2)*treatment)

summary(lme2.diag.ide.REML)

plot(lme2.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.), id=0.05, adj=-0.1)  

plot(lme2.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.) | treatment, id=0.05, adj=-0.1) 
plot(lme.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.), id=0.05, adj=-0.1)

qqnorm(lme.diag.ide.REML, ~ resid(.))

lme2.diag.ide.REML <- update(lme.diag.ide,method="REML", ~.+I(day^2)*treatment)

summary(lme2.diag.ide.REML)

plot(lme2.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.), id=0.05, adj=-0.1)  

plot(lme2.diag.ide.REML, resid(., type='p') ~ fitted(.) | treatment, id=0.05, adj=-0.1) 


The qqnorm plot shows a quite straight line except for the tail. Therefore, the modelling seems not too bad. The standardized residuals plot exhibits a pattern; the middle part of fitted values have larger residuals compared to the two sides. This implies that a quadratic term of may be helpful to improve the model fitting (you may try this).

5.2. Justify whether the predicted random effects are normally
distributed (for example check the qqnorm plot).











Random effects are not residuals: use `qqnorm(fit, ~ ranef(.))`. You are
checking the assumption b_i ~ N(0, G).




qqnorm(lme.diag.ide.REML, ~ ranef(.), id=0.1, adj=-0.2)
qqnorm(lme.diag.ide.REML, ~ ranef(.), id=0.1, adj=-0.2)


The qqnorm plots of both the random intercept and slope are close to a straight line, so it seems reasonable to assume the random effects are normally distributed.

5.3. Give the 95\% confidence intervals for the estimates of fixed effects and
variance components. Explain whether or not they are significant.











`intervals()` returns confidence intervals for fixed effects, variance
components and correlation parameters in one call. An interval for a variance
that nearly touches zero is telling you something.

text:
Week 5 — Generalised estimating equations






NoteHow to use this page





Each exercise below is a live R session. Type your answer and press Run; you can experiment freely, nothing is saved and nothing can break. The first block takes a few seconds to start while R loads in your browser.
Worked solutions are on Canvas.



























In a study of the effects of vitamin A deficiency in preschool children (available in the course package as ichs), 250 children were examined at an initial clinic visit and again at 3 month intervals for a year (at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 months after the first visit). The investigators are particularly interested in assessing whether or not the children with vitamin A deficiency are at increased risk of developing respiratory infection. At each examination, the presence or absence of respiratory infection, the child’s age in years, gender, and whether they suffered from vitamin A deficiency are recorded. The ICHS data file has the following columns:

Let \(Y_i\) be the vector of responses for the \(i\)th child, consisting of the elements \(Y_{ij}\), which are observations on whether the child has a respiratory infection at time \(t_{ij}\) (recorded in months; Yes=1 and No=0). Write down a model for \(E(Y_{ij})\) with an appropriate link function that is linear in an intercept and additive terms for time, age, gender, and vitamin A status. Also, write down \(\mbox{Var}(Y_{ij})\) given the nature of the response.

\(Y_{ij} \in \{0,1\}\) records whether child \(i\) has a respiratory infection at time \(t_{ij}\), so \(Y_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu_{ij})\) with \(\mu_{ij} = E(Y_{ij}) = P(Y_{ij} = 1)\).
Because \(\mu_{ij}\) must lie in \((0,1)\) while a linear predictor ranges over the whole real line, we need a link function. The natural choice for a binary response is the logit, the canonical link for the Bernoulli:
\[\text{logit}(\mu_{ij}) = \log\!\left(\frac{\mu_{ij}}{1-\mu_{ij}}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Time}_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Age}_{ij}
+ \beta_3 \text{Gender}_i + \beta_4 \text{VitA}_{ij},\]
for \(i = 1,\dots,250\) and \(j = 1,\dots,6\).
Interpretation: each \(\beta_k\) is a log odds ratio. In particular \(\exp(\beta_4)\) is the odds of infection for a vitamin A deficient child divided by the odds for a sufficient child, holding time, age and gender fixed. \(\beta_3\) is time-constant (gender does not change), while time, age and vitamin A status vary within a child.
For the variance, a Bernoulli variable has variance determined entirely by its mean — there is no free dispersion parameter:
\[\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = E(Y_{ij}^2) - \{E(Y_{ij})\}^2
= \mu_{ij} - \mu_{ij}^2 = \mu_{ij}(1 - \mu_{ij}),\]
using \(Y_{ij}^2 = Y_{ij}\) for a 0/1 variable. So the variance function is \(v(\mu) = \mu(1-\mu)\), maximal at \(\mu = 1/2\) and shrinking towards zero as \(\mu\) approaches 0 or 1.
In practice one often allows a scale (dispersion) parameter \(\phi\),
\[\text{Var}(Y_{ij}) = \phi\,\mu_{ij}(1 - \mu_{ij}),\]
with \(\phi > 1\) indicating overdispersion and \(\phi < 1\) underdispersion relative to the Bernoulli. For genuinely binary data \(\phi\) is not identifiable from a single observation, but it becomes meaningful once repeated measurements are pooled, and GEE estimates it as a moment-based scale factor.
What this model does not yet do. It specifies only the mean and the variance of each individual observation. It says nothing about the association between \(Y_{ij}\) and \(Y_{ik}\) for two visits on the same child. Fitting it as though all \(1500\) observations were independent ignores that association — which is exactly what part 2 asks you to do, and what part 3 asks you to repair.

Fit the model in part (1) without taking the within-subject correlation into account, i.e., taking all the observations from the children as if they were independent. Based on this fit, is there any sufficient evidence to suggest that the mean pattern of respiratory response is associated with the presence or absence of vitamin A deficiency? State the null hypothesis corresponding to this question in your model (a), describe the test statistic and p-value on which you draw the conclusion, and state your conclusion.

working correlation is `corstr = "independence"`.
The response is binary, so `family = binomial`, and `id = ID` tells the function
which rows belong to the same child.
Look at the Wald test for the vitamin A coefficient.

level,
we do not have evidence to reject $H_0$. We then conclude that the mean 
pattern of respiratory response is not associated with the presence or 

Write down a model that extends the model in part (1) by taking into account the within-subject correlation among repeated measurements.

Extend the model by keeping the same marginal mean but adding a model for the within-child association. This is the generalised estimating equations (GEE) formulation.
Let \(\mathbf{Y}_i = (Y_{i1},\dots,Y_{in_i})^{\mathrm{T}}\) be the responses for child \(i\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i\) the corresponding mean vector. The mean model is unchanged:
\[\text{logit}(\mu_{ij}) = \mathbf{x}_{ij}^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{\beta}.\]
The covariance of \(\mathbf{Y}_i\) is written as
\[\text{Var}(\mathbf{Y}_i) = \mathbf{V}_i
= \phi\,\mathbf{A}_i^{1/2}\,\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\,\mathbf{A}_i^{1/2},\]
where

\(\mathbf{A}_i = \text{diag}\{\mu_{i1}(1-\mu_{i1}),\dots,\mu_{in_i}(1-\mu_{in_i})\}\) holds the Bernoulli variance function on its diagonal;
\(\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is the working correlation matrix, depending on a small parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\);
\(\phi\) is the scale parameter.

Common choices for \(\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\):



Structure
Form
Parameters




Independence
\(\mathbf{I}\)
none


Exchangeable
\(\text{corr}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}) = \alpha\), \(j \neq k\)

AR(1)
\(\text{corr}(Y_{ij},Y_{ik}) = \alpha^{|t_{ij}-t_{ik}|}\)
1


Unstructured
all pairs free
\(n(n-1)/2\)



\(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is estimated by solving the estimating equations
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf{D}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{V}_i^{-1}
(\mathbf{Y}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i) = \mathbf{0},
\qquad \mathbf{D}_i = \frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathrm{T}}}.\]
Two properties make this worth doing, and they are the heart of the week:

\(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\) is consistent even if \(\mathbf{R}_i(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\) is wrong, provided the mean model is right. The working correlation need only be a working assumption.
The naive standard errors are not robust to that misspecification. Valid inference uses the sandwich (robust, empirical) estimator \[\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) =
\mathbf{H}^{-1}\left\{\sum_i \mathbf{D}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{V}_i^{-1}
(\mathbf{Y}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_i)(\mathbf{Y}_i-\boldsymbol{\mu}_i)^{\mathrm{T}}
\mathbf{V}_i^{-1}\mathbf{D}_i\right\}\mathbf{H}^{-1},
\qquad \mathbf{H} = \sum_i \mathbf{D}_i^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{V}_i^{-1}\mathbf{D}_i.\]

Note that the interpretation of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is marginal — a population-averaged log odds ratio, comparing groups of children — not subject-specific as it would be in a GLMM with random effects. The two are not equal for a logit link, and the distinction matters when reporting.
Try run_app("gee_robustness") to see points 1 and 2 happen: with an exchangeable truth and an independence working correlation, the slope stays unbiased while the naive standard error is badly wrong and the robust one is not.

Fit your model in part (3) to the data. Assuming that your model for the within-subject correlation is correct, conduct a hypothesis test for the null hypothesis in part (2). State your conclusion. Does the result agree with that in part (2)? Based on the results from your R output, give an explanation for your conclusion. Provide a summary of your model selection and justify your choice.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 8 tutorial
text:
Week 8 — Kriging and spatial prediction
In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Galicia dataset, often used in geostatistical analysis, refers to lead concentration data from a network of 121 meteorological stations across the Galicia region in Northwest Spain. The Galicia dataset has the following columns:
Three calls to `glgpm()`. The formula controls all three differences:
`loglead ~ gp(kappa = 1.5)` for the first, add `nugget = NULL` inside `gp()` to
estimate a nugget, and put `pm10 +` before `gp()` to add the covariate.
Watch what happens to the nugget estimate and to its confidence interval.
# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)


# Fitting a Linear geostatistical model

# Model 1 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + S(xi ),
model1 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ gp(kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)

summary(model1)

# Fitting a Linear geostatistical model

# Model 2 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + S(xi ) + Z_i,
model2 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ gp(nugget = NULL, kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)
summary(model2)

# Model 3 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + \beta1 xi,1 + S(xi ),
model3 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ pm10  + gp(kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)

summary(model3)
       # Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)
library(RiskMap)

# Load the data

# Create a spatial object
galicia_sf <- st_as_sf(galicia, coords = c("long", "lat"), crs= 4326)

crs_galicia <- propose_utm(galicia_sf)
galicia_sf <- st_transform(galicia_sf, crs = crs_galicia)


# Fitting a Linear geostatistical model

# Model 1 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + S(xi ),
model1 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ gp(kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)

summary(model1)

# Fitting a Linear geostatistical model

# Model 2 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + S(xi ) + Z_i,
model2 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ gp(nugget = NULL, kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)
summary(model2)

# Model 3 - log(Yi ) = \beta0 + \beta1 xi,1 + S(xi ),
model3 <- glgpm(formula = loglead ~ pm10  + gp(kappa = 1.5), 
                family = "gaussian",
                data = galicia_sf)

summary(model3)
How did adding \(x_{i, 1}\) affect the estimates of the covariance parameters?
The three fits give:
Model (2) versus model (1): the nugget adds nothing. The estimate is \(\hat\tau^2 = 0.00087\), about 2.7% of the spatial variance, with a confidence interval of \([0, \infty)\) — completely uninformative. The log-likelihood is identical to model (1) to four decimal places, so the likelihood ratio statistic is essentially zero on 1 degree of freedom. The extra parameter buys no fit.
This is what you should expect from the design rather than a surprise. The nugget captures variation at distances shorter than the closest pair of points, plus measurement error. With 132 stations spread across Galicia there are very few near-neighbour pairs, so the data carry almost no information at short range and the nugget is close to unidentifiable. The lesson is that a nugget is estimable only if the design contains close pairs — which is an argument for including some deliberately when you plan a survey.
Model (3) versus model (1): the covariate helps, with a caveat. PM10 has \(\hat\beta_1 = 0.0114\) with a Wald \(p\)-value below 0.001, and the log-likelihood rises from 179.12 to 180.80.
But the two tests disagree, and it is worth being honest about it:
The Wald test treats the covariance parameters as known at their estimates. The likelihood ratio test allows them to be re-estimated under each model, and here they change noticeably (see item 3), so the LRT is the more trustworthy of the two. On that basis the evidence for PM10 is suggestive rather than decisive.
Conclusion. Model (3) is the one to prefer: it has the highest likelihood, it is no more complex than model (1) in its covariance structure, and PM10 is a scientifically plausible predictor of lead deposition since both are products of traffic and industry. Model (2) should be discarded — it is model (1) with an unidentifiable extra parameter. A defensible alternative answer is to prefer model (1) on the grounds that the LRT for PM10 does not reach 5%; what matters is that the reasoning is stated.
`coef()` gives the estimated parameters. The two to interpret are the spatial
process variance and the correlation scale phi.
Phi is not itself the distance at which correlation dies away — convert it to a
practical range, the distance at which correlation falls to about 0.05. For a
Matern with kappa = 1.5 that is roughly 4.7 times phi; solve it properly with
`uniroot()`.
par_hat <- coef(model3)
par_hat
practical_range <- uniroot(function(x) matern_cor(x, phi = par_hat$phi, kappa = 1.5) - 0.05,
        lower = 0.001, upper = 100)$root
practical_range
par_hat <- coef(model3)
par_hat
practical_range <- uniroot(function(x) matern_cor(x, phi = par_hat$phi, kappa = 1.5) - 0.05,
        lower = 0.001, upper = 100)$root
practical_range
Prediction needs a grid (`galicia_grid`) and, for the model with the covariate,
the covariate at each grid point (`galicia_pred`).
Map both the predicted mean and the standard error. The second map is the one
that tells you where to trust the first.
predictors <- galicia_pred
grid_pred <- galicia_grid %>% 
  st_as_sf(., coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = crs_galicia) %>% st_as_sfc()


# Predict linear predictor
pred_S_lb1 <- pred_over_grid(model1, grid_pred = grid_pred,
               predictors = predictors)

# Predict T(x)

pred_T_lb1 <- pred_target_grid(pred_S_lb1,
                pd_summary = list(mean = mean,
                                  std_err = sd))


plot(pred_T_lb1, 
     which_summary = "mean",
     main = "Predictive mean")

plot(pred_T_lb1, 
     which_summary = "std_err",
     main = "Predictive standard error")
# Predict linear predictor
pred_S_lb3 <- pred_over_grid(model3, grid_pred = grid_pred,
               predictors = predictors)

# Predict T(x)

pred_T_lb3 <- pred_target_grid(pred_S_lb3,
                pd_summary = list(mean = mean,
                                  std_err = sd))


plot(pred_T_lb3, 
     which_summary = "mean",
     main = "Predictive mean")

plot(pred_T_lb3, 
     which_summary = "std_err",
     main = "Predictive standard error")
predictors <- galicia_pred
grid_pred <- galicia_grid %>% 
  st_as_sf(., coords = c("X", "Y"), crs = crs_galicia) %>% st_as_sfc()


# Predict linear predictor
pred_S_lb1 <- pred_over_grid(model1, grid_pred = grid_pred,
               predictors = predictors)

# Predict T(x)

pred_T_lb1 <- pred_target_grid(pred_S_lb1,
                pd_summary = list(mean = mean,
                                  std_err = sd))


plot(pred_T_lb1, 
     which_summary = "mean",
     main = "Predictive mean")

plot(pred_T_lb1, 
     which_summary = "std_err",
     main = "Predictive standard error")
# Predict linear predictor
pred_S_lb3 <- pred_over_grid(model3, grid_pred = grid_pred,
               predictors = predictors)

# Predict T(x)

pred_T_lb3 <- pred_target_grid(pred_S_lb3,
                pd_summary = list(mean = mean,
                                  std_err = sd))


plot(pred_T_lb3, 
     which_summary = "mean",
     main = "Predictive mean")

plot(pred_T_lb3, 
     which_summary = "std_err",
     main = "Predictive standard error")
Both models produce very similar mean prediction surfaces: the same broad pattern of high predicted log-lead in the areas where high values were observed, and the same smooth decay away from them. This is expected, because in both cases the prediction is dominated by the observed data through kriging, and the covariate shifts the mean surface only modestly.
The differences show up in two places.
First, the model with PM10 borrows strength from the covariate in areas where data are sparse. Where there are few stations, model (1) reverts to the overall mean \(\hat\beta_0\), whereas model (3) reverts to \(\hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1
\times \text{PM10}\) at that location. So the two surfaces differ most where the sampling is thinnest and PM10 departs from its average.
Second, the prediction standard errors are slightly smaller for model (3) almost everywhere, because part of the variation is now explained by a measured covariate rather than left in the residual spatial process: \(\hat\sigma^2\) falls from 0.0323 to 0.0304.
Against that, model (3)’s shorter correlation scale (\(\hat\phi\) falls from 9.02 to 7.86 km, a practical range of 37 km against 43 km) means the process is “forgotten” more quickly with distance, so the advantage narrows far from the data. Adding a covariate does not uniformly reduce uncertainty; it trades residual variance against a shorter range of borrowing.
Requiring the covariate for prediction is also a practical cost: model (3) can only predict where PM10 is known, which is why the exercise supplies a covariate surface on the prediction grid.

title: Spatial data analysis: week 8 tutorial
text:
Challenge
Use the Liberia data from the RiskMap package to build a binomial geostatistical model to investigate the relationship between log elevation and onchocerciasis prevalence in Liberia.. The dataset can be called in R using data(liberia). This data-set contains counts of reported onchocerciasis (or riverblindess) cases from 91 villages sampled across Liberia. The variables are as follows:

lat latitude of the of sampled villages.
long longitude of the sampled villages.
ntest number of tested people for the presence nodules.
npos number of people that tested positive for the presence of nodules.
elevation the elevation in meters of the sampled village.
log_elevation the log-transformed elevation in meters of the sampled village.

Predictive uncertainty is lowest close to the sampling stations, and particularly where several stations are clustered together. It is highest in the gaps between stations and around the edges of the study region, where prediction becomes extrapolation.
The reason is in the kriging variance. For a Gaussian process the prediction variance at a location \(x_0\) is
\[\text{Var}\{S(x_0)\mid \mathbf{Y}\} = \sigma^2 -
\mathbf{c}_0^{\mathrm{T}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\mathbf{c}_0,\]
where \(\mathbf{c}_0\) holds the covariances between \(x_0\) and the observed locations. When \(x_0\) is close to data, the entries of \(\mathbf{c}_0\) are large, the quadratic form subtracts a large amount from \(\sigma^2\), and the variance is small. As \(x_0\) moves away, the correlations decay towards zero, \(\mathbf{c}_0
\to \mathbf{0}\), and the variance rises towards the prior variance \(\sigma^2\) — the model has nothing to say beyond the overall mean.
Two consequences worth drawing out:

The distance that matters is set by \(\hat\phi\). With a practical range of about 43 km for model (1), a prediction location more than roughly that far from any station is effectively uninformed by the data. This is why the map of standard errors looks like a set of low-uncertainty basins around the station network.
Uncertainty maps are as important as prediction maps. A predicted value in a data-sparse region may look identical to one in a well-sampled region, but it is far less trustworthy. Presenting the mean surface without the standard error surface invites over-confident conclusions — and if the question of interest is whether lead exceeds some threshold, the answer should be given as an exceedance probability, which uses both.

In this tutorial sheet, you will learn the following:
We analyse the Lip cancer data in scotland. The data contain, for each of the Scotland counties, the number of observed and expected lip cancer cases among males in Scotland between 1975-1980, and a variable that indicates the proportion of the population engaged in agriculture, fishing, or forestry (aff). The aff variable is related to exposure to sunlight which is a risk factor for lip cancer. The data also contain the shapefile of the Scotland counties and everything can be found in scotland_lip

Two steps. First build the adjacency matrix from the polygons, as in week 9 —
and note the geometry is in metres, so a `snap` tolerance must be in metres too.
Then `S.CARleroux()` with `family = "poisson"`, the AFF covariate, and
`offset(log(expected))`.
The offset is what turns a count model into a relative risk model: without it
you would be modelling raw counts rather than counts relative to what is
expected.

library(spdep)
library(sf)
scot <- scotland_lip
W.nb <- poly2nb(scot, row.names = scot$county, snap = 200000)
W <- nb2mat(W.nb, style = "B")
model.car <- S.CARleroux(formula= cases ~ aff + offset(log(expected)), family="poisson",
 data=scot,
W=W, rho=0, burnin=2000, n.sample=10000, thin=8,
verbose=FALSE)
print(model.car)

We start by reading the shapefile of Scottish counties into an sf object, which allows spatial operations in R. Then defines the neighbours between regions using shared polygon boundaries. The argument snap = 200000 is crucial for this dataset because some Scottish counties are islands or separated by narrow channels. Without snap, R might fail to detect neighbours that are visually close but not touching. The snap = 200000 allows neighbouring polygons within 200 map units to be treated as adjacent. This improves connectivity in the spatial model by including islands or nearby coastal regions that should logically share risk structure. Then we converts the neighbour list to a binary adjacency matrix, where 1 indicates a neighbour, 0 otherwise. Then we fit the model such that - Outcome: cases = number of lip cancer cases - Offset: log(expected) adjusts for varying expected counts - Covariate: aff = ecological risk factor - Random Effects: spatial effects via Leroux CAR model and note that rho = 0 implies a model with CAR structure.

`model$samples$fitted` holds the posterior samples, so the posterior mean gives

Then we calculate the relative risk (RR) and RR > 1 implies higher than average risk and RR < 1 implies lower than average risk. Above, we show the map of the RR and the posterior standard deviation (SD) of RR to show uncertainty in the estimates. The comparison plot shows how modelling (with spatial structure) can moderate extreme SIR values. SIR: direct estimate of risk from observed data (can be noisy). RR (posterior): smooths noisy data using the model, borrowing strength from neighbours. ### Challenge

Map the probability that the relative risk is greater than 2.











You have posterior samples of the relative risk, so the probability that it
exceeds 2 is just the proportion of samples above 2, computed area by area.
This is the kind of statement a public health decision actually needs: not a
point estimate, but how confident we are that risk is elevated.




# Extract posterior samples of fitted values (mu_i)
fitted_samples <- model.car$samples$fitted  # matrix: samples x areas

# Convert to posterior samples of relative risk
RR_samples <- fitted_samples / matrix(scot$expected, nrow = nrow(fitted_samples), ncol = length(scot$expected), byrow = TRUE)

# For each area, calculate P(RR > 2)
scot$RR_gt2 <- apply(RR_samples, 2, function(x) mean(x > 2))

library(ggplot2)
library(viridis)

ggplot(scot) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = RR_gt2)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0.8, 0.8)) +
  scale_fill_viridis(name = "P(RR > 2)", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  ggtitle("Posterior Probability that RR > 2") +
  theme_minimal()

This shows the certainty that a county’s risk is more than twice the average. P(RR > 2) = 1 implies Very likely high-risk and P(RR > 2) = 0 implies Low certainty or not high-risk. This is particularly useful for flagging high-risk areas in public health settings.

Same call, but the ICAR model is the limiting case with `rho` fixed at 1 — see
`S.CARleroux`'s arguments. Compare the fitted risks: ICAR assumes the spatial
structure is entirely local, so it tends to smooth more.
